paper_title: Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in a Nigerian Cohort

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: High-resolution brain MRI is important for neuroradiological assessment, yet routine clinical protocols often rely on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions, particularly in resource-constrained settings. These acquisitions may differ in orientation, alignment and anatomical coverage, resulting in partially overlapping image stacks. Existing learning-based super-resolution methods typically rely on single, under-constrained inputs or fixed multi-stack configurations with idealised acquisition geometry. We introduce MS-HVED, a sequence-agnostic framework for flexible multi-stack brain MRI super-resolution. Available axial, coronal and sagittal stacks are independently encoded into multi-scale Gaussian posteriors and fused using a field-of-view-aware Product-of-Gaussians formulation that limits contributions from unsupported regions. Physics-informed domain randomisation simulates heterogeneous clinical acquisition conditions, including obliqueness, partial coverage and imaging artefacts. MS-HVED achieved competitive or superior reconstruction fidelity across synthetic benchmarks and improved downstream tissue segmentation relative to low-resolution inputs. To assess generalisation beyond the training cohorts, we performed external clinical validation on 30 routine brain MRI examinations from a Nigerian cohort, representing an under-represented population in medical imaging research. These examinations formed the largest component of a blinded reader study involving 44 real cases and seven expert neuroradiologists. In the Nigerian cohort, MS-HVED was preferred over the supervised baseline for overall image quality in 187 of 210 paired assessments. Across all clinical cohorts, MS-HVED achieved higher overall-quality scores with all available inputs (5.93 vs. 4.49, p<.001), with the preference persisting when axial or coronal inputs were omitted (p<.001). Introduction High-resolution isotropic brain MRI is important for accurate diagnosis, surgical planning, and longitudinal monitoring of neurological disease [30, 46]. In routine clinical practice, and particularly in resource-constrained settings where scanner availability, patient throughput, and acquisition time are major constraints, brain MR examinations are often conducted with fast 2D multi-slice protocols with thick slices, employed to keep scan time low, mitigate motion, and maintain signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) [2, 30, 46]. Page 1 of 27 Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in Nigerian Cohort these protocols achieve high in-plane resolution, they suffer from poor through-plane resolution, producing anisotropic 3D stacks that hinder volumetric analysis and multi-planar review. To partially compensate for this limitation, clinical protocols commonly acquire multiple stacks across axial, coronal and sagittal orientations [2]. Super-resolution reconstruction (SRR) seeks to recover single isotropic high-resolution (HR) volume from one or more anisotropic low-resolution (LR) stacks. Multi-stack SRR exploits complementary content of orthogonal acquisitions, where each stack provides high-fidelity information in its in-plane directions while lacking the throughplane detail [17, 46]. The central methodological challenge is therefore to fuse these incomplete, orientation-specific observations into geometrically consistent volumetric representation, ideally without per-subject optimisation or expensive iterative slice-to-volume registration. The classical line of work formulates SRR as modelbased inverse problem solved by iterative slice-to-volume registration and optimisation [14, 17, 53, 54]. These methods are well established in fetal MRI, where extreme inter-slice motion makes registration dominant difficulty. However, they are computationally expensive and can be brittle in heterogeneous adult cohorts and low-resource clinical settings, where fast 2D acquisitions remain the norm. Learningbased SRR methods can be broadly divided into supervised and self-supervised methods. Supervised models are trained once on paired LR-HR datasets and then applied directly to new scans [11, 22]. However, many learned SRR methods operate on single anisotropic stack, making the reconstruction problem severely under-constrained in the throughplane direction and potentially prone to blurring, loss of fine structure, or hallucinated anatomy [23, 28, 47]. Beyond the through-plane ambiguity, single-stack reconstruction is also limited by the anatomical extent of the selected acquisition. In routine clinical protocols, axial, coronal and sagittal stacks may be prescribed with different partial fields-of-view (FOVs) [2, 29]. Consequently, anatomy or pathology that is absent from one orientation may still be visible in another. For example, an axial stack prescribed with limited superior-inferior coverage may exclude an extraaxial lesion near the vertex, whereas the same lesion may be captured in the sagittal stack. This type of orientationspecific variation in anatomical coverage is shown in the appendix (Figure A.8). method that reconstructs from the axial stack alone cannot recover such clinically relevant information, regardless of its super-resolution capacity. This motivates multi-stack SRR methods that exploit complementary orientation-specific coverage rather than treating each stack in isolation. Self-supervised learned reconstruction methods such as SMORE [57], ECLARE [39] and TripleSR [41] reduce the need for paired supervised training data by optimising model using only the available anisotropic scan. However, these approaches typically require computationally heavy per-subject optimisation at inference and therefore do not provide single reusable model that can immediately reconstruct arbitrary subsets of axial, coronal and sagittal inputs. Flexible fusion of missing or incomplete inputs has been studied in multi-modal segmentation, including HeMIS [21] and U-HVED [12], but analogous flexibility remains less explored for multi-stack MRI super-resolution, where the absence arises not only from absent input orientations but also from spatially varying FOV within each orientation. We introduce MS-HVED, flexible hetero-orientation variational framework for multi-stack brain MRI superresolution. As shown in Figure 1, each available orientation is encoded independently into latent multi-scale Gaussian posterior, and the available posteriors are fused using Product-of-Gaussians (PoG). Because fusion is defined over the set of available orientations, the same network can reconstruct from any non-empty subset {Ax, Cor, Sag} at inference. This allows the model to use one, two or three input stacks without retraining or changing the network architecture. This flexible fusion is paired with explicit modelling of the acquisition geometry encountered in real clinical multistack scans. Axial, coronal and sagittal stacks are rarely perfectly aligned with canonical reference frame. Each stack may be prescribed at an oblique angle, and after registration to common isotropic grid the resampled stack can occupy rotated and partially valid grid, with invalid or weakly supported regions near the volume boundaries. simple preprocessing workaround is to trim poorly supported edge slices after resampling, but this is heuristic outside the reconstruction model and often discards useful measurements. MS-HVED instead makes stack prescription part of both training and inference, specifically, the forward model simulates acquisition obliqueness and partial-FOV, and the fusion module receives per-orientation FOV masks that modulate each stacks precision contribution at the voxel level. Evaluating multi-stack MRI super-resolution is also challenging. Synthetic LR-HR experiments provide known references and controlled acquisition geometry, but may not fully capture the mismatch observed in real clinical data. Paired real LR-HR acquisitions provide more realistic reference, but are scarce and when available, the LR and HR scans are acquired separately and may differ in contrast, intensity scale, motion state, etc. Finally, many clinically important datasets have no matched isotropic HR reference, requiring qualitative, expert-reader or task-based evaluation. We therefore evaluate MS-HVED using complementary protocols: full-reference quantitative metrics on synthetic benchmarks, blinded expert-reader evaluation on reference-free clinical cohorts as well as downstream tissuesegmentation analysis. Across multiple experiments, MS-HVED achieves best or competitive reconstruction quality while retaining flexibility across input configurations. Ablation experiments show that oblique partial-FOV simulation and FOV-aware fusion are important for robust reconstruction under realistic acquisition geometry. We avoid activation normalisation layers in the reconstruction backbone to preserve intensity relationships between the inputs and reconstructions, and stabilise posterior prediction using spectral normalisation. 5. We evaluate reconstruction fidelity, missing-orientation robustness, sequence-agnostic generalisation, downstream segmentation utility and clinical image quality, providing comprehensive assessment than voxelwise similarity metrics alone. 6. Single-stack MRI super-resolution Convolutional super-resolution networks were introduced for natural images by [11] and have since been transferred to MRI. Jurek et al. [26] apply 3D CNNs to recover isotropic resolution from single thick-slice acquisition. SMORE [57] achieves anti-aliasing and through-plane super-resolution from single anisotropic volume in selfsupervised framework by exploiting the higher resolution of in-plane patches. ECLARE [39] extends this idea by Muhammad et al. Page 3 of 27 Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in Nigerian Cohort estimating the slice excitation profile via ESPRESO [19] and training per-subject network on cross-planar in-plane patches. More recent arbitrary-scale approaches use implicit or explicit neural representations to handle variable slice spacing [37, 48], and diffusion models have been adapted to brain and body MRI SR with mechanisms to reduce sampling cost [20, 58]. While powerful, single-stack methods remain intrinsically limited by the information available in the selected acquisition [4, 5, 46]. First, through-plane detail is underconstrained when only one anisotropic view is observed. Missing high-frequency structure must be inferred from learned priors or within-stack context, which can lead to blurring, hallucinated anatomy, or contrast inversions on out-of-distribution clinical data [4, 5]. Second, and more importantly for routine multi-orientation protocols, single stack is limited by its anatomical extent. If pathology or structure lies outside the prescribed FOV of the selected stack, it cannot be recovered by any single-stack SR method. complementary line of work pre-trains generative priors and uses them at inference. SynthSR [23] demonstrates that aggressive domain randomisation, i.e. sampling contrasts, resolutions, and artefacts from vast distributions during training, enables strong cross-domain generalisation in single feed-forward pass, but the model still operates on single stack at inference. InverseSR [47] formulates SR as latent-diffusion inversion using 3D brain-MRI prior, and MRIFlow [28] uses normalising flow with frequency prior. These methods produce sharp reconstructions, but they require iterative inference or learned prior over target distribution and do not provide natural mechanism for fusing complementary information from multiple anisotropic stacks. 2.2. Multi-stack MRI super-resolution Multi-stack super-resolution and slice-to-volume reconstruction (SVR) have been studied extensively in fetal MRI, where extreme inter-slice motion makes registration the dominant difficulty. Classical optimisation based pipelines [14, 17] explicitly model the acquisition forward problem and alternate between volume reconstruction and slice-to-volume registration. They produce high-quality reconstructions but are computationally expensive and sensitive to registration failures, limiting their scalability to large heterogeneous clinical cohorts. Learning-based variants speed up the registration step using transformers [54], replace the volume parameterisation with implicit neural representations [53], or learn slice-profile conditioned generative networks [32]. Most recently, [22] learn multi-view interpolation weights for fetal-brain SRR. In adult brain MRI, where inter-slice motion is typically more moderate, several works specifically address learned multi-stack reconstruction. TripleSR [41] fuses two orthogonal anisotropic stacks using an implicit neural representation trained with sparse coordinate-based loss in continuous space. It is self-supervised and effective in its two-view setting, but it performs computationally heavy per-subject optimisation and does not directly support third stack or missing input orientation within one reusable model. Recent supervised orthogonal-scan methods also show the value of combining complementary anatomical views with 3D CNNs [42], but they still assume fixed input set. This motivates evaluating fixed-input baselines alongside flexible model that can operate on arbitrary subsets of axial, coronal and sagittal stacks. Most learning-based multi-stack SRR studies simplify either the input availability problem or the acquisition geometry. In the first case, models are trained for fixed set of orientations and cannot directly adapt when one orientation is absent. In the second case, stacks are often treated as axisaligned fully overlapping volumes. However, real clinical stacks may be obliquely prescribed and may provide only partial FOV. 2.3. Hetero-modal and probabilistic fusion The idea of fusing variable subsets of inputs through shared probabilistic latent space comes from multi-modal segmentation. HeMIS [21] aggregates per-modality features using first and second-order statistics, supporting any nonempty subset of input modalities. U-HVED [12] reformulates this idea as hetero-modal variational encoder-decoder where each modality contributes Gaussian posterior to shared latent space through Product-of-Experts fusion, and single trained model performs joint segmentation and modality completion under arbitrary subsets of available modalities. Although these hetero-modal approaches provide useful mechanism for handling missing input channels, they were developed primarily for segmentation problems rather than geometric super-resolution. In those setups, missingness is treated at the input level where modality is either available or absent. Multi-stack SRR introduces an additional spatial form of missingness because of the anatomical extent of the inputs. 2.4. Domain randomisation major obstacle to supervised SRR is the scarcity of paired LR-HR clinical data. Domain randomisation, popularized in robotics [43] and adapted for medical imaging by SynthSR [23] and SynthSeg [6], addresses this problem by training on synthetic data generated from broad distributions over contrast, resolution, and artefacts, on the premise that sufficiently randomized training distribution covers the true clinical distribution as special case. In MRI super-resolution, domain randomisation has most often focused on intensity contrast, resolution, noise, bias fields, and other appearance level or degradation level factors. These components are important for cross dataset robustness, but they do not fully capture the geometry of routine multi-stack acquisitions. Existing randomisation strategies therefore leave gap between synthetic LR generation and the spatial patterns observed in clinical multi-orientation protocols. This motivates randomisation schemes that model not only image degradation, but also acquisition geometry and orientation-specific FOV. Muhammad et al. Evaluation and benchmarking of MRI super-resolution Benchmarking MRI super-resolution is challenging because reconstruction quality is not fully captured by single metric. Full-reference measures such as PSNR, SSIM, MAE/RMSE and normalised cross-correlation are useful when HR reference is available, and remain widely used in MRI reconstruction, synthesis and super-resolution studies. However, voxel-wise and structural metrics can favour overly smooth reconstructions, are sensitive to intensity normalisation and spatial misregistration, and may not reflect the preservation of clinically relevant anatomy [1, 10]. Perceptual or feature-based metrics provide complementary information about sharpness and structural plausibility, but they are often derived from natural-image feature spaces and should be interpreted cautiously in medical imaging [1, 55]. In addition, high image-level similarity does not necessarily imply improved clinical or downstream utility, such as tissue segmentation, lesion assessment or diagnostic confidence [3, 56]. Most MRI SR studies therefore use combination of full-reference quantitative metrics and qualitative assessment. Early and recent learning-based SR methods commonly report PSNR, SSIM, RMSE/MAE or related measures on synthetically downsampled data, where an HR target is known by construction [26, 39, 41, 57]. Other studies evaluate on paired LR-HR acquisitions [13], which better reflect real imaging conditions but introduce pseudoreference problem: the HR scan is acquired separately and may differ in contrast or noise. In such cases, quantitative scores measure similarity to the available HR acquisition rather than absolute reconstruction accuracy. Several MRI SR and accelerated reconstruction studies have therefore incorporated expert reader studies to assess clinical image quality directly. Chaudhari et al. [8] evaluated musculoskeletal MRI SR using both quantitative metrics and radiologist reader study, with readers assessing sharpness, contrast, artefacts, SNR and overall diagnostic quality. Ebner et al. [13] evaluated upper-abdominal MR super-resolution reconstruction with expert readers, reporting subjective preference and anatomical clarity scores for clinically relevant structures. In brain MRI, Rudie et al. [40] prospectively evaluated deep learning-based resolution enhancement using four board-certified neuroradiologists who scored SNR, anatomic conspicuity, overall image quality, artefacts and diagnostic confidence on Likert scale. These studies show that expert review is often needed when the relevant endpoint is diagnostic interpretability rather than numerical agreement with reference image. Task-based evaluation provides another complementary route. In medical image SR, Zhang et al. [56] showed that improvements in conventional image-quality metrics do not necessarily translate into improved signal-detection, motivating evaluation against clinically or analytically meaningful tasks. More recent biomedical SR benchmarks have similarly assessed whether SR improves downstream segmentation or classification rather than only image similarity [3]. Together, these works suggest that robust SR evaluation should combine full-reference metrics where valid references exist, qualitative or expert assessment where references are unavailable or imperfect, and downstream task evaluation where the reconstructed images are intended to support automated analysis. 3. The encoder and decoder are built from residual blocks without activation normalisation layers, using LeakyReLU activations and residual scaling [31]. Group, instance, and batch normalisations, which are common in segmentation backbones, are intentionally omitted because they can distort the absolute intensity scale needed for MRI SR. Stability is instead provided by residual scaling, free-bits KL regularisation [27], and spectral normalisation (Section 3.3). 3.3. Spectrally normalised variational head The encoder and decoder are built without activation normalisation layers such as batch, instance or group normalisation. This design choice is motivated by the regression nature of MRI super-resolution, where the network must preserve absolute and relative intensity relationships in the reconstructed image. However, removing activation normalisation also removes common source of training stabilisation. This is particularly important in variational architecture, where the encoder predicts voxel-wise Gaussian parameters rather than deterministic features alone. High-capacity variational encoder-decoders can be difficult to train because the posterior parameterisation must remain both expressive and well regularised. Small perturbations in the predicted log-variance can lead to large changes in the posterior precision and KL divergence [9], while overly expressive decoders or poorly balanced KL terms can encourage posterior collapse, where the latent variables carry little information about the input [49]. We therefore use two complementary stabilisation mechanisms: spectral normalisation [34] to constrain the encoders that predict Gaussian parameters, and free-bits KL regularisation [27] to reduce posterior collapse. We apply spectral normalisation to the convolutional layers in the residual pathways and to the 111 variational projections. Spectral normalisation acts on the layer weights rather than on the intermediate feature activations. It constrains the operator norm of the corresponding mapping and therefore limits the sensitivity of the predicted posterior mean and log-variance to small perturbations in the input features. Although spectral normalisation was introduced for stabilising GAN discriminators [34], we use it here for its weight-level effect rather than for any adversarial objective. Importantly, spectral normalisation is not used as replacement for batch, instance or group normalisation. Those methods normalise feature activations and may alter intensity statistics, whereas spectral normalisation constrains selected weights without normalising the feature maps themselves.

Crucially, the obliqueness is recorded in the LR stacks affine matrix(and therefore propagates through the resampling step 𝑈𝑘). At fusion time, the resampled LR stack appears in the canonical frame as rotated, partially out-of-bounds volume. This is the same geometry that real oblique acquisitions present after registration to common reference, and it is the geometry that the FOV mask of Section 3.4 is designed to handle. We do not explicitly simulate residual registration error in the current implementation. This is limitation of the present model and is revisited in the discussion. 3.5.2. Partial-FOV support simulation We simulate partial coverage by suppressing peripheral slices along the through-plane axis while preserving randomly sampled central coverage fraction. In our experiments the retained fraction is sampled between 40% and 70% of the native LR stack, with coverage constraint that prevents all stacks from being simultaneously truncated. The resulting binary FOV map 𝑏𝑘(𝐱) is recorded alongside the stack and passed to the FOV-aware fusion module. For evaluation on real clinical inputs, 𝑏𝑘(𝐱) is computed deterministically by resampling the native stack support into the reference grid (see Section 3.7). 3.5.3. The KL term corresponds to the freebits multi-scale KL term defined in Equation (4). 𝑘 The perceptual term perc is implemented as 2.5D AlexNet-based feature loss. Perceptual losses compare images in the feature space of pretrained CNN and better capture visually relevant differences than purely voxelwise objectives in reconstruction and synthesis [25, 55], including MRI reconstruction [16]. We compute the feature distance on 2D slices sampled from the reconstructed and reference volumes, following recent 2.5D perceptual supervision for volumetric medical images [35], because fully 3D perceptual losses are memory intensive and require suitable pretrained 3D feature extractors. Page 7 of 27 Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in Nigerian Cohort 4.2. Datasets 4.2.1. Source MRI cohorts Three high-resolution (HR) brain MRI cohorts were used as source data for training and synthetic evaluation. The first was an internal meningioma cohort (MEN) comprising 774 T1-weighted volumes acquired under heterogeneous clinical protocols. The second and third were the publicly available IXI T1-weighted and T2-weighted cohorts [24]. The internal cohort was split into 537110127 training/validation/test cases, while the IXI T1-weighted and T2-weighted cohorts comprised 4068887 and 4048886 training/validation/test volumes, respectively. The internal clinical data were accessed under the AIdriven Management of Brain Tumours (AIMBraTS) study, approved by the NHS Research Ethics Committee (REC reference: 22/NS/0160; IRAS ID: 320754). Individual patient consent was not required because the study involved retrospective analysis of routinely collected clinical data. All internal data were handled in accordance with the UK Data Protection Act 2018 [44] and UK General Data Protection Regulation [45]. The IXI dataset is publicly available and was used in accordance with its data-access conditions. All HR volumes were defaced [15], resampled to 1mm isotropic resolution using trilinear interpolation, and intensitynormalised to [0, 1]. 4.2.2. Synthetic LRHR data The HR volumes described above were used to generate synthetic anisotropic LR stacks using the physicsinformed forward model in Section 3. For each HR volume, axial, coronal and sagittal stacks were generated with randomised acquisition parameters, including anisotropic resolution, oblique prescription, partial-FOV coverage and image artefacts. The original HR volume served as the reference target for supervised training or full-reference quantitative evaluation depending on which split they were assigned to. 4.2.3. Real evaluation cohorts To assess generalisation to real multi-stack acquisitions, we evaluated MS-HVED on three additional cohorts. The first consisted of 7 paired LRHR T2-weighted healthycontrol brain MRI cases from Ebner et al. [13]. The HR acquisition is used as pseudo-reference for quantitative evaluation, because the LR and HR scans are necessarily acquired with different acquisition settings. Consequently, differences in contrast, intensity scale and image appearance may reflect acquisition-physics mismatch rather than reconstruction error alone. This 7 cases were also included in the expert-reader study, allowing the reference-based and subjective assessments to be interpreted together. The second cohort consisted of 7 low-resolution multistack meningioma cases from our institution, acquired under the AIMBraTS study approval described above (REC reference: 22/NS/0160; IRAS ID: 320754). These cases contain clinically relevant tumour pathology but do not have matched 3D HR reference acquisitions. In this cohort, 6 Muhammad et al. of the 7 cases contain only two orientations, providing realistic test for missing orientation. The third cohort was drawn from the publicly available Nigerian clinical MRI dataset [51, 52]. The full dataset contains scans from 35 healthy participants, 31 individuals with age-related dementia and 22 individuals with Parkinsons disease, with T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR and DWI acquisitions. We used 30 cases (consisting of T1weighted, T2-weighted and FLAIR images) from this cohort as an additional reference-free clinical generalisation test, reflecting acquisition and population characteristics distinct from the training cohorts. For all real evaluation cohorts, the available LR stacks were rigidly registered to common reference space and resampled to 1, mm isotropic resolution. When no matched HR reference was available, the reconstruction grid was defined by the union of the available LR stack supports. 4.3. Implementation details MS-HVED is implemented in PyTorch [38] and trained on single NVIDIA A100 GPU. We use the AdamW [33] optimiser with learning rate 104 and weight decay 105, cosine annealing schedule with 5% linear warm-up, and mixed-precision training. Training is run for up to 1000 epochs with early stopping, using patches of size 12812864 and batch size of 2. Free-bits is set to 𝛽fb=1 nat per scaleaggregated KL term. Spectral normalisation is applied to the convolutional residual pathways and to the variational projections. Default loss weights are fixed across all experiments: 𝑤rec = 0.4, 𝑤ori = 0.4, 𝑤kl = 0.1, 𝑤ssim = 0.1, 𝑤perc = 0.1. Domain-randomisation transforms are implemented using PyTorch [38] and MONAI [7]. To evaluate sequence-agnostic training, we trained three dataset-specific MS-HVED models independently on the IXI-T1, IXI-T2 and MEN training sets, and fourth model on the combined training data. The sequence-agnostic model therefore encountered both T1and T2-weighted images and data from different acquisition cohorts during training, while retaining the same architecture, loss function and optimisation settings as the dataset-specific models. At evaluation, the shared model was tested separately on each heldout cohort and compared with the corresponding datasetspecific model. For FOV-aware fusion, each stack is associated with binary mask 𝑏𝑘(𝐱) 0, 1, where 1 denotes voxels inside the spatial coverage of orientation 𝑘 and 0 denotes voxels outside it. For synthetic data, this support map is obtained directly from the simulated stack geometry. For real data, it is computed by resampling the native stack support into the common reconstruction grid. At each latent scale 𝑠, the binary mask is downsampled and smoothed with an isotropic Gaussian kernel: 𝑚𝑘,𝑠(𝐱) = (𝑔𝜎 𝑏𝑘 ) (𝐱𝑠), (10) Page 8 of Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in Nigerian Cohort where 𝑔𝜎 has standard deviation 𝜎=3 voxels and 𝐱𝑠 denotes the coordinate at scale 𝑠. SegResNet was trained separately for each dataset and input configuration (AX, AX+COR, and AX+COR+SAG), whereas single MSHVED model per training setting accepted every non-empty orientation subset. On the paired real cohort, we additionally evaluated NiftyMIC [13, 14] as representative classical approach and naive baseline in the form of non-learned FOV-weighted average (Naive+FOV) computed by: 𝑋mean+FOV(𝐱) = 𝑘 𝑚𝑘(𝐱)𝑌𝑘(𝐱) 𝑘 𝑚𝑘(𝐱) , (11) Here, 𝑌𝑘 is the registered stack and 𝑚𝑘 is its FOV-derived contribution weight. 4.4.2. Quantitative metrics Quantitative evaluation of MRI super-resolution is not straightforward because different metrics capture different aspects of reconstruction quality. Voxel-wise errors such as mean absolute error (MAE) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) measure numerical agreement with reference image, but they may favour smooth reconstructions and can be sensitive to small contrast differences. 3D structural similarity (SSIM) [50] provides complementary measure of local structural similarity, while perceptual losses are more sensitive to image sharpness and feature-level differences. For this reason, we report multiple metrics rather than relying on single score. On synthetic data, we report MAE, PSNR, SSIM, and the 2.5D AlexNet-based perceptual loss. Metrics are computed over the HR target region captured by the input stacks used by each method, as described below: Let 𝑀𝑜 denote the FOV mask for orientation 𝑜 {AX, COR, SAG}. For method using the orientation set , metrics are computed over 𝑀 = 𝑜 𝑀𝑜. Thus, single-stack axial methods are evaluated only over 𝑀AX, dual-stack methods such as TripleSR and MS-HVED AX+COR are evaluated over 𝑀AX 𝑀COR, and threestack methods are evaluated over 𝑀AX 𝑀COR 𝑀SAG, corresponding to the full HR target region captured by the available synthetic acquisitions. This avoids penalising method for anatomy outside its input FOV while still evaluating reconstruction fidelity over the region it could in principle reconstruct. On the paired healthy-control real cohort, we report PSNR, SSIM, normalised cross-correlation (NCC), and perceptual loss against the HR pseudo-reference. Since the LR where 𝑎 and 𝑏 are estimated by ordinary least squares. This calibration removes global linear intensity differences, allowing PSNR and SSIM to better reflect spatial and structural agreement. NCC is also reported because it is insensitive to global linear intensity variations. To assess whether image-level improvements translate to improved downstream analysis, we evaluate tissue segmentation performance on the synthetic test sets. SynthSeg [6] is applied to the axial LR inputs, SegResNet reconstructions and MS-HVED reconstructions. Segmentations obtained from the corresponding HR volumes are used as reference segmentations. We evaluate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), grey matter (GM), and white matter (WM) using Dice score and the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95, in mm). This provides task-oriented evaluation of whether the reconstructed images preserve anatomical structures relevant to automated brain analysis. 4.5. Expert-reader study Reference-free clinical evaluation is necessary for the real cohorts because no isotropic HR reference is available. In these cohorts, image quality is assessed by expert review using blinded side-by-side rating protocol. Seven boardcertified neuroradiologists were shown SegResNet and MSHVED reconstructions in random order with method labels hidden. Cases were reviewed on dedicated interface that allows multi-planar inspection of the reconstructed volumes and comparison against the available LR inputs. screenshot of this interface is provided in Figure A.1. Experts score each reconstruction on 19 ordinal scale for the following criteria: freedom from artefact, signal-tonoise ratio (SNR), sharpness, visibility of tumour pathology where applicable, and overall image quality. Reconstructions were assessed in pairs, and readers were not permitted to assign the same score to both methods for given case and criterion, thereby requiring directional preference while retaining the ordinal rating scale. This introduces forced choice component analogous to pairwise and two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) assessment [18]. All criteria were scored with higher values indicating better image quality. The pathology-visibility criterion was applied only to cases with visible focal pathology, i.e. the meningioma cohort, and was marked not applicable for the others. Input availability was tracked separately from cohort. In some cases, one or more stacks were unavailable, so they could not be used for reconstruction or displayed in the review interface. In other cases, an axial or coronal stack was available and remained visible to the reader in the interface, but was deliberately omitted from both reconstruction methods to test performance with missing input. Results 5.1. Synthetic dataset evaluation As summarized in Table 1, MS-HVED was competitive across all three synthetic test cohorts. With three inputs, it obtained the best MAE, PSNR, SSIM, and perceptual loss on MEN. It also achieves the best MAE, PSNR, and SSIM on IXI-T1, with perceptual loss tied, and the second-best values on IXI-T2, where three-input SegResNet performed best. When tested on two inputs, MS-HVED still remained competitive with fixed-input baselines, particularly for SSIM on MEN and IXI-T1. Representative synthetic reconstructions are shown in Figure 2. 5.1.1. Flexible orientation handling The same MS-HVED model was evaluated with two additional dual-input combinations. As shown in Table 2, performance was similar for AX+SAG and COR+SAG on every test cohort. Across the three cohorts, the absolute PSNR difference between these input combinations was at most 0.75 dB. These results support the intended use of one model with different available orientation subsets, without retraining separate network for each subset. 5.1.2. Sequence-agnostic reconstruction As shown in Table 3, sequence-agnostic training remained competitive with dataset-specific training. It improved PSNR and perceptual loss on IXI-T1 and MEN, and achieved the lowest perceptual loss on IXI-T2. The datasetspecific models retained higher SSIM on IXI-T1 and IXI-T2 and higher PSNR on IXI-T2. Thus, shared model reduced the need for contrast/sequence specific training while maintaining comparable performance across cohorts. 5.1.3. Ablation study We ablate the two geometric components introduced to make MS-HVED robust to realistic multi-stack acquisition settings: oblique and partial-FOV of simulated datasets, and FOV-aware mask in PoG fusion. The first component exposes the model to stacks whose spatial supports are rotated, incomplete and only partially overlapping, matching the geometry commonly observed in clinical multi-orientation acquisitions. The second component provides voxel-wise information during fusion, allowing the model to distinguish between valid low-resolution evidence and regions where an orientation does not contribute anatomical information. As presented in Table 4, oblique partial-FOV simulation produced the largest improvement, and FOV-mask conditioning provided further consistent benefit. Relative to the variant with neither component, the complete model improved PSNR by 6.06, 5.89, and 4.46 dB on MEN, IXIT1, and IXI-T2, respectively. Adding the masks to the FOVsimulated model further improved SSIM by .014.049 and reduced perceptual loss by .031.039. 5.1.4. Downstream evaluation We assess downstream utility using SynthSeg [6] on the synthetic test cases, treating the segmentations of the HR volumes as reference segmentations. Dice score and the 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95, in mm) for CSF, GM, and WM are presented in Table 5, with representative case visualized in the appendix (Figure A.4). Both learned reconstructions markedly improved SynthSeg performance relative to single LR input  (Table 5)  . MSHVED and SegResNet had nearly identical Dice scores on IXI-T1 and IXI-T2. On MEN, MS-HVED improved CSF Dice from .86 to .87 and reduced HD95 for CSF, GM, and WM. 5.2. Real-data evaluation 5.2.1. Paired real cohort The 7 paired real cases permitted comparison with separately acquired HR pseudo-reference. As presented in Table 6, the FOV-weighted stack average achieved the highest PSNR, SSIM, and NCC. These metrics tend to favour smoother reconstructions with strong voxel-wise and structural agreement, and may therefore not fully reflect perceptual sharpness or preservation of fine anatomical detail. MSHVED achieved the lowest perceptual loss and improved over SegResNet in every reported metric. However, the HR images were separate acquisitions rather than exact ground truth. We therefore retained these full-reference results and complemented them with expert ratings of the same seven cases in Section 5.3. 5.2.2. Discussion This study demonstrates that MS-HVED can reconstruct isotropic brain MRI from variable subsets of anisotropic multi-orientation stacks while accounting for the spatial extent of each acquisition. Across complementary evaluations, the method achieved competitive or leading reconstruction fidelity, preserved downstream tissue-segmentation performance, and was preferred to SegResNet by expert neuroradiologists when evaluating real clinical data. 6.1. Acquisition-aware fusion improves robustness to clinical geometry Geometric ablation provides the clearest evidence for the importance of acquisition-aware modelling. Introducing oblique and partial-FOV simulation during training increased PSNR by 4.466.06 dB compared with training without realistic acquisition geometry. Incorporating FOV masks produced further improvements, particularly in SSIM and perceptual loss. These components address related but distinct sources of variation. The domain-randomisation pipeline exposes the model to rotated, incomplete, and partially overlapping acquisitions during training, whereas the FOV masks determine where each orientation should contribute during fusion. MS-HVED supports variable orientations, contrasts, reconstruction grids, and stochastic inference key benefit of MS-HVED is that one trained model can operate on different subsets of axial, coronal and sagittal stacks. The model maintained similar performance across AX+COR, AX+SAG and COR+SAG configurations without requiring separate network for each input combination, unlike fixed-input supervised baselines. This flexibility is important for retrospective and clinical datasets, where stacks may be absent because of protocol differences, incomplete examinations, motion corruption or acquisition failure. The sequence-agnostic experiment demonstrated related trade-off. single model jointly trained on IXIT1, IXI-T2, and MEN remained competitive with datasetspecific models and improved several PSNR, MAE, and perceptual results, although it did not achieve the best result for every metric. Additionally, since MS-HVED is fully convolutional, its inference is not tied to fixed grid. model trained using 1mm isotropic targets can therefore be evaluated on finer reconstruction grid, e.g. 0.5mm. We demonstrate this resolution flexibility across acquisitions with different native resolutions and field strengths in Section A.5. Lastly, the variational formulation of MS-HVED provides an additional capability beyond the deterministic reconstructions evaluated. At inference, the fused multi-scale posterior can be decoded at its mean, as used for all reported experiments, or sampled repeatedly to produce stochastic multi-sample reconstructions. Repeated samples can expose regions in which the reconstruction is sensitive to latent uncertainty. This is particularly relevant where one or more orientations are missing or have limited coverage. Establishing such dispersion as calibrated measure of reconstruction uncertainty will require dedicated validation, nevertheless, multi-sample inference follows directly from the fused posterior and does not require change to the trained architecture. Muhammad et al. Page 16 of Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in Nigerian Cohort 6.3. Full-reference metrics do not capture all reconstruction artefacts The experiments highlight the limitations of conventional full-reference metrics for MRI super-resolution. MAE, PSNR and SSIM are useful for controlled synthetic evaluation, but they aggregate errors over the reconstructed volume and may hide localised boundary or wedge-shaped artefacts. This helps explain why SegResNet was competitive on several simulated benchmarks, while expert readers identified poorer image quality. These localised errors include altered signal intensity, loss of anatomical separation, and reduced conspicuity of small structures. 6.4. Expert assessment provides evidence on real clinical image quality The blinded reader study extends the evaluation beyond simulated degradation models and imperfect pseudoreferences. Seven expert neuroradiologists assessed 44 cases from the paired healthy, Nigerian, and meningioma cohorts. MS-HVED received higher overall-quality ratings than SegResNet when all available stacks were used and retained its advantage when axial or coronal inputs were withheld. Improvements were also observed for artefact, SNR, and anatomical consistency, while differences in sharpness were less pronounced. This pattern suggests that the preference for MS-HVED was not driven solely by apparent sharpness, but also by cleaner and more anatomically coherent reconstructions. The accompanying reader comments provide further insight into the types of residual errors present in both methods. Figure 5 shows examples of these errors with reader comments. In one healthy-control case, the interpeduncular cistern appeared abnormally dark in both reconstructions, indicating failure shared by the two learned approaches. In meningioma case with no sagittal input, the spinal cord was poorly delineated in both reconstructions, although SegResNet showed more pronounced artefacts. Readers also identified several local anatomical inconsistencies in the Nigerian cohort: increased signal within the genu of the corpus callosum in SegResNet reconstruction, conflation of the left ICA flow void with adjacent structures in both methods but more prominently with SegResNet, and reduced separation between the pituitary gland and clivus in another SegResNet case. These observations complement the quantitative ratings by showing that residual reconstruction errors can be spatially localised and anatomically specific, and may therefore have limited influence on global image-similarity metrics. 6.5. Limitations and future work Several limitations remain. First, MS-HVED assumes that the available stacks have been rigidly registered and resampled to common space before fusion. Residual misregistration can introduce inconsistent anatomical evidence that the fusion mechanism cannot fully correct, and registration error is not explicitly simulated during training. Second, although the reader study included multiple acquisition sources, the clinical meningioma cohort contained only seven cases and therefore represented limited range of tumour appearances and imaging protocols. Larger multiinstitutional studies are needed to assess robustness across scanners, field strengths, contrasts, pathologies and acquisition quality, and to determine whether improvements in reconstructed image quality translate into improved diagnostic interpretation. The reader comments also indicate that acquisitiondomain shift warrants further investigation. Row (D) of Figure 5 shows Nigerian case acquired at 0.3,T, both methods showed reduced separation of the left ICA flow void from adjacent structures, with the artefact more pronounced for SegResNet. Since the training cohorts consisted predominantly of 1.5,T and 3,T acquisitions, differences in SNR and image characteristics at low field may have contributed to this failure. Future work should therefore include dedicated low-field training and evaluation data. Finally, the discrepancy between competitive simulated metrics and expert observations of local anatomical errors highlights the need for SRR metrics that are sensitive to boundary artefacts, altered signal, anatomical separation and pathology preservation. The stochastic posterior available in MS-HVED may also provide useful uncertainty information, but its calibration and clinical relevance require dedicated validation. 7. Conclusion MS-HVED provides flexible variational framework for reconstructing isotropic brain MRI from the available subset of anisotropic axial, coronal, and sagittal image stacks. Its combination of oblique partial-FOV simulation and spatially aware Product-of-Gaussians fusion allows the model to use valid information from each orientation without assuming identical extent or requiring separately trained network for every input configuration. Across synthetic and real (paired and reference-free) clinical evaluations, MS-HVED achieved competitive reconstruction fidelity, preserved downstream tissue segmentation performance, and received higher expert ratings than SegResNet for overall image quality. The reader preference persisted across the Nigerian, meningioma, and paired healthy cohorts and when an axial or coronal input was deliberately omitted. The variational posterior additionally permits stochastic multi-sample inference, providing basis for future evaluation of reconstruction stability and uncertainty. These results support MS-HVED as robust approach for heterogeneous multi-stack brain MRI. Future multiinstitutional evaluation will extend the range of datasets and pathologies, address registration-related failures, and determine whether the observed improvements translate into greater diagnostic accuracy and clinical utility.
